title: ML Infra Trade-offs at Scale
summary: The cross-cutting infrastructure trade-offs interviewers probe across every ML system design question, once the model itself is settled.

Fraud scoring at checkout must be online — the transaction is happening right now. A weekly "recommended for you" email can be entirely batch — precomputed overnight, no request-time inference at all. Getting this wrong in either direction either blows your latency budget or wastes serving cost on freshness nobody needed.

slides.sectionTitle: Latency budgets across a multi-stage pipeline
slides.markdown:
Every multi-stage system (candidate generation → ranking → re-ranking, seen across feed, search, and recommenders) shares one total **latency SLA** that has to be split across stages. If the whole request must finish in 200ms, retrieval might get 50ms, ranking 100ms, re-ranking and rendering the rest — and each stage's model complexity is bounded by its slice of that budget, not by what would be most accurate in isolation.

This is why retrieval-stage models are deliberately simpler than ranking-stage models — it's not a modeling preference, it's a hard constraint imposed by the shared latency budget.

As training data grows past what fits on one machine, training has to **distribute** — splitting data across workers (data parallelism) or splitting the model itself across devices (model parallelism, needed once a model is too large for one GPU's memory). See [ml-pipelines-versioning](ml-pipelines-versioning) for how this fits into the broader pipeline.

The practical decision point: distribute only once single-machine training is genuinely the bottleneck (too slow to iterate, or literally doesn't fit) — the added complexity of synchronizing gradients across workers, or debugging a sharded model, is real overhead you shouldn't pay before you need to.

| | Hosted model API | Train your own |
|---|---|---|
| Time to ship | Fast — integrate and go | Slow — data, training, evaluation, serving infra |
| Cost at scale | Per-call pricing can dominate at high volume | High upfront cost, cheaper marginal cost at scale |
| Customization | Limited to what the API exposes | Full control over features, latency, architecture |
| Data sensitivity | Data leaves your infrastructure | Stays in-house |

**How to decide:** a hosted API is usually right to validate a product idea fast or at modest volume; training your own earns its cost once you're at genuine scale, need tight latency control, or have sensitive data that can't leave your infrastructure.

slides.sectionTitle: Handling scale spikes and stale models
slides.markdown:
Two failure modes worth naming explicitly in any design: a **traffic spike** that exceeds serving capacity, and a **stale model** that's fallen behind (a deployment failed, or retraining is delayed). The standard mitigation for both is the same principle: **graceful degradation** — fall back to a simpler, cheaper heuristic (recent popularity, a cached previous result, a rule-based default) rather than serving errors or blocking the request entirely.

A system that fails open to "good enough" under stress is almost always preferable to one that fails closed and serves nothing — this is the kind of resilience thinking interviewers specifically listen for.

For a global product, serving a model close to the user (multi-region deployment) cuts network latency, but introduces the same consistency questions as any distributed system (see consistency-and-replication topics in the System Design area): do all regions serve the exact same model version, and how quickly does a new model roll out everywhere?

A common compromise: replicate the (already-trained) model artifact to every region for low-latency inference, while keeping training centralized in one region — inference needs to be close to users, but training doesn't need to be, since it's not latency-sensitive in the same way.
